strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: MP-Bench contains 421,363 aligned pairs of raw ERA5 4D meteorological data (time x 37 pressure levels x lat x lon) and CMA severe-weather warning text from 2,412 stations (2023-2024), covering seven weather types with severity levels and four QA formats. This is a genuinely large and carefully curated resource that fills a real gap noted in Table 1 relative to CrisisLex, ClimBench, WeatherQA, OmniEarth-Bench, etc.

Sensible architecture: MMLM ingests 4D meteorological tensors directly rather than flattening/projecting them into RGB images, explicitly avoiding the information loss the authors identify in prior work. The three plug-and-play modules map cleanly onto the temporal (DTGF), spatial (TGS), and vertical/channel (TGCA) dimensions, and the ablation (Table 3) shows each contributes (e.g., all three together: MC-main 57.23 vs. 42.73 baseline).

Broad evaluation across four task types (MC, T/F, RSW, NSW) and comparison to four open-source MLLMs plus GPT-4o, with per-weather-type analysis (Fig. 5) and interpretability analysis (Figs. 6, 8, 9) that ties learned weights to physical processes (e.g., peak humidity sensitivity at 950 hPa, geopotential at 150 hPa).
Clear practical motivation: automated severe-weather warning generation has real value for disaster mitigation, and the paper grounds the problem well in operational forecasting practice.
weaknesses: The GPT-4o comparison is not fair and does not support the headline claim. GPT-4o receives a 3-channel vectorized meteorological input while MMLM receives the full 4D 185-channel field with three specialized modules. The conclusion that GPT-4o "exhibits severely limited performance" is therefore confounded by the input-representation mismatch, not a clean test of the model's capability. No experiment equalizes the input across systems.

The "prediction" framing is questionable. The input window is [t, t+11] where t is the warning issuance time, i.e., reanalysis data contemporaneous with (and partly after) the warning. Since ERA5 reanalysis already assimilates observations of the event, the model is closer to detecting/reading off conditions during the event than forecasting it. No experiment uses data strictly prior to t, so the "end-to-end AI forecasting/warning" claims are overstated.

NSW, the most comprehensive generation task, scores only 2.1/5 and the paper neither diagnoses this failure in depth nor reconciles it with the claim of "performing exceptionally well across multiple tasks." The most practically relevant task is essentially unsolved.

Limited methodological novelty: DTGF (adjacent-frame gating, Eqs. 1-3), TGS (Gaussian coordinate masking, Eqs. 4-6), and TGCA (channel attention, Eqs. 7-9) are all standard techniques; the contribution is primarily application-level and dataset-level rather than architectural.

No comparison to established AI weather-forecasting or NWP baselines (Pangu, GraphCast, FuXi, etc., all cited in related work), so the practical advantage of MMLM over existing operational systems is not established.

Reproducibility and rigor gaps: code and dataset are only promised ("will be made publicly available"), the QA-generation and negative-sampling procedures are thinly described, results appear to be single-run without variance/error bars, and class imbalance (snow storm ~1.7%; gale >40% in Table 2 of the appendix) is acknowledged but not fully mitigated.
Geographic scope is limited to China, and generalization is only demonstrated within one country; cross-region transfer is not tested.

strengths: The MP-Bench dataset is a substantial and novel resource: 421,363 pairs of raw ERA5 4D meteorological fields (time x 37 pressure levels x longitude x latitude, 5 variables) aligned with CMA severe-weather warning texts, covering 7 severe weather types over 2023-2024. This scale and the retention of vertical/temporal resolution (12-hour window starting at warning issuance time) meaningfully improves on prior datasets that collapse fields into daily means or RGB images (cf. Table 1 comparison with WeatherQA, CLLMate, ClimateIQA).

The core modeling idea of ingesting raw 4D meteorological data into an MLLM rather than compressing to 2D RGB or daily averages is a well-motivated departure from prior work (CLLMate, WeatherQA, OmniEarth-Bench) and is the paper's clearest technical novelty.

The three plug-and-play modules (DTGF, TGS, TGCA) are each motivated by a distinct physical/structural property of the data (temporal abruptness, geographic grounding, channel redundancy across 185 input channels), and the ablation in Table 3 supports their complementarity (e.g., MC-sub 28.01 -> 36.01 with all three; T/F 58.47 -> 79.21).

Interpretability analysis is a genuine plus: Fig. 6 and Fig. 8/9 show learned weight distributions consistent with meteorological expectations (humidity peaked at 950 hPa, geopotential at 150 hPa, U-wind at 350 hPa, V-wind at 125 hPa, higher temporal gating weight in the first hours for red warnings). This is more than a black-box accuracy report and supports the credibility of the modules.

The QA task taxonomy (MC with severity sub-levels, T/F, Region-SW, National-SW) spans multiple spatial granularities and output formats, and the appendix prompt templates make the task design concrete and replicable.

The paper is generally well organized: dataset statistics, alignment strategy, module formulations (Eqs. 1-9), training hyperparameters (Table 3 in appendix), and detailed experimental settings are reported, which aids reproducibility relative to typical dataset papers.
weaknesses: The baseline comparison is not informative about the method's actual advantage. Table 2 compares MMLM (Qwen2.5-VL-7B + DTGF/TGS/TGCA) against other open-source backbones that are also 'enhanced with three plug-and-play modules,' so the table primarily demonstrates backbone choice, not the value of the proposed pipeline over prior MLLM-for-weather methods. There is no comparison against CLLMate, WeatherQA, or other prior multimodal weather models on MP-Bench, despite these being the natural points of reference in Related Works.

The GPT-4o comparison is a handicapped baseline: GPT-4o is given only a 3-channel input (2m temperature, 10m u/v wind, total precipitation), which discards the 37 pressure levels, the temporal window, and two of the five ERA5 variables. Interpreting its low scores as evidence of 'inability to handle meteorological question answering' conflates input-modality mismatch with model capability, and weakens the central claim that MMLM is necessary.

The RSW evaluation is ambiguous. The prompt (Fig. 3 in appendix) asks the model to 'identify which types of severe weather events may occur, selecting from the following categories,' which is a multi-label task, yet the evaluation section states accuracy is computed by selecting 'one of eight weather categories.' This mismatch between task definition and metric can systematically mis-score correct multi-event predictions, and no clarification of how multi-label outputs are scored is provided.

The NSW task relies entirely on GPT-4o as an LLM judge with a 0-5 rubric, with no human validation, no inter-annotator agreement, no comparison to an automated matching metric, and no analysis of judge bias (e.g., verbosity/length effects). Given NSW's low absolute scores (1.1-2.1 out of 5) and the sensitivity of conclusions to the judge, this is a material measurement concern.

The dataset is China-only and temporally limited to 2023 training / 2024 testing. The abstract's claim of 'nationwide scope, year-round coverage' is accurate only within China, and the paper does not analyze geographic or temporal distribution shift, nor whether the model generalizes to unseen years or regions. This constrains the generality claim implied by 'a key step toward realizing automated AI-driven weather forecasting systems.'

Several architectural and data-pipeline details that determine whether the method is actually feasible at scale are underspecified in the main text: how the parallel module outputs are tokenized/compressed before entering the LLM, the resulting token count per sample, how 37 pressure levels x 5 variables x 12 timesteps are reduced to LLM input dimensionality via '3D convolutional layer + MLP,' and whether the LLM backbone weights are frozen (only LoRA, rank 8). These details are needed to judge whether the model genuinely 'directly ingests 4D meteorological data' or performs aggressive compression.

Class imbalance is acknowledged but not addressed methodologically: snowstorm is ~1.7% of samples and snowstorm accuracy is <=6% across all models, yet no re-weighting, sampling, or cost-sensitive training is evaluated. The 'normal weather' negatives are artificially sampled (49,660 entries), which may introduce a distributional bias into the T/F and MC tasks that is not analyzed.

No uncertainty quantification or statistical testing is reported for the main comparisons (e.g., confidence intervals or significance tests on Table 2), and 'MC-sub' is used as a headline metric without an explicit definition in the main text.

strengths: A genuinely large-scale and carefully specified multimodal resource: 421,363 aligned samples (371,703 CMA warnings + 49,660 normal) spanning seven severe-weather categories, 2,412 stations, nationwide and year-round coverage, with a temporally disjoint 2023 train / 2024 test split.

The dataset preserves 4D structure (hourly ERA5 at 0.25 degrees, 5 variables across 37 pressure levels, 12-hour windows) instead of collapsing to daily means or RGB images, which is a real improvement over prior severe-weather multimodal datasets such as CLLMate, WeatherQA and ClimateIQA; Table 1 makes the distinction explicit.

The three plug-and-play modules are simple and the ablation in Table 3 shows each one helps individually, with the full parallel combination giving the largest gains (MC-main 42.73 to 57.23, T/F 58.47 to 79.21); the interpretability analyses (Figure 6, appendix Figure 8/9) show weight peaks at physically plausible levels (e.g., specific humidity at 950 hPa, U-wind at 350 hPa, geopotential at 150 hPa), suggesting the modules learn non-trivial structure.

The paper is clearly organized, and the appendix supplies the exact prompts for all four QA types, the GPT-4o scoring rubric, and the full training/evaluation hyperparameter table, which materially helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central framing is unsupported by the experimental design. The input window is [t, t+11] hours starting at the warning issuance time t, i.e., the model is fed the atmospheric state during and after the period for which the warning was issued. This makes the benchmark a retrospective detection/attribution task, not prediction or early warning. The stated operational scenario (ingesting NWP output available before issuance) is never tested, so the abstract's claim of an end-to-end 'AI severe weather system' with 'timely and accurate' warnings is not established.

No ablation removes the meteorological input. There is no text-only / location-plus-date baseline, even though the warning corpus carries very strong geographic and seasonal priors (gale is 40-43% of all warnings; July is the peak month; Figure 3, appendix Table 2 and Figure 6). Without such a baseline it is impossible to tell whether MMLM interprets ERA5 fields or merely exploits spatiotemporal priors learned from the prompt.

The baseline comparison is confounded and does not isolate the contribution. GPT-4o is given only a hand-crafted 3-channel input (2 m temperature, 10 m u/v wind, total precipitation) and is not fine-tuned, whereas the open-source models receive the full 185-channel 4D tensor and are LoRA-tuned; moreover, Table 2's caption states that all open-source models are already 'enhanced with three plug-and-play modules'. The table therefore contains no true un-augmented baseline, and yet GPT-4o's low scores are used as evidence for 'the critical necessity of the proposed MMLM.'

No domain-appropriate baseline is provided. Since the task reduces to classifying severe weather from reanalysis fields, a simple CNN/MLP or physical threshold classifier on ERA5 is the natural strong baseline. Its absence means the paper does not show that an MLLM is a better choice than a much simpler model for this problem.

The T/F metric as reported is uninformative. The class balance of the 42,933 T/F questions is never given; if it mirrors the overall corpus (~88% warning vs. ~12% normal), then the reported 87.13% T/F accuracy is indistinguishable from always answering 'Yes'. Similarly, RSW 'accuracy' of 67.46% is reported without stating whether the underlying task is single-label or multi-label.

The multiple-choice design forces exactly one correct answer among 25 options, but multiple warnings frequently co-occur for the same station and time (e.g., rainstorm plus gale). Ground truth is therefore ambiguous and a correct prediction can be scored as wrong; the paper neither discusses this simplification nor quantifies its impact.

The NSW task is scored entirely by GPT-4o against an ad hoc 0-5 rubric, with no human agreement study, no inter-rater reliability check, and no validation that the LLM judge is stable. The absolute result is low (2.1/5), and Table 2 mixes two different scales (0-100 and 0-5) in one block of numbers.

Technical novelty is modest and the method is under-specified. DTGF (gating from adjacent-frame differences), TGS (Gaussian mask around query coordinates) and TGCA (text-conditioned channel attention) are standard components applied to a new modality. The TGCA equations do not pin down dimensions or semantics of P, v and X, and it is unclear how 185 channels are mapped into the vision encoder or how the 3D-convolution fusion and MLP are configured.

Claims are overstated relative to the evidence. 'Performs exceptionally well' is not supported by MC-sub 58.19, RSW 67.46 and NSW 2.1/5, and the assertion that this is 'the first time that MLLM has been used to deeply interpret raw meteorological data' is contradicted by cited prior work (CLLMate, WeatherQA, ClimateIQA, OmniEarth-Bench, Chen et al. 2024a).

Presentation and rigor issues: the introduction lists 'RSW Questions and RSW Questions' instead of NSW; MC-main and MC-sub are used in every table but never defined in the main text; the appendix reuses 'Figure 5' for a different (CoE) figure than the main-text Figure 5; no variance, error bars or multiple runs are reported for any metric; and the dataset/code is only promised, with the availability and licensing of the CMA warning records left unclear.

strengths: Introduces MP-Bench, a large-scale multimodal dataset for severe weather event prediction with 421,363 pairs, seven severe weather types plus normal weather, nationwide coverage in China, and four QA task types. This addresses a real scarcity of multimodal meteorological benchmarks.

Develops MMLM with three plug-and-play modules (DTGF, TGS, TGCA) designed for 4D meteorological data, including temporal, spatial, and vertical pressure-level feature extraction. The architecture is plausible and tailored to the domain.

Reports consistent improvements of MMLM variants over baseline VLMs on MP-Bench tasks (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B MC-main 72.37 vs. 56.26) and provides an ablation study showing each module contributes on a 5,000-sample subset.

Includes supplementary analyses such as temporal window ablation, visualizations of module weights, physically motivated channel attention patterns, and a cross-geographical generalization test on 1,000 U.S. NOAA samples.
Provides detailed training and evaluation hyperparameters (Tables 8-9), which supports reproducibility if the dataset and code are released.
weaknesses: Temporal leakage undermines the core forecasting claim: inputs are ERA5 fields from [t, t+11] starting at warning issuance time t, so the model sees the future period during which the warned event is expected to occur. This is retrospective classification/detection, not forecasting. The finding that longer windows improve performance (Table 4) is consistent with leakage rather than genuine predictive skill.

Uses ERA5 reanalysis, which is not available at operational warning issuance time. Real-time early warning requires NWP forecasts or current observations, so the claimed automated early-warning pipeline is not operationally realistic.

Ground-truth labels are CMA severe weather warnings, not observed severe weather events. Warnings are subjective forecasts/alerts and may include false alarms and misses; the dataset therefore measures warning reproduction rather than actual severe weather event prediction. No verification against station observations or damage records is provided.

Baseline comparisons are confounded: GPT-4o and open-source baselines are given only 3-channel/3-pressure-level meteorological inputs, while MMLM uses 185 channels and three additional modules. Gains may reflect increased input dimensionality and extra parameters rather than the proposed fusion modules. A controlled experiment with identical high-dimensional inputs without modules is missing from the full evaluation.

Evaluation lacks standard meteorological verification metrics (e.g., POD, FAR, CSI) and comparisons to specialized NWP or severe weather detection models. The T/F task reports only accuracy without majority-class baselines or precision/recall, and the NSW score is low (2.1/5) and judged by GPT-4o, which is also used as a baseline model.

Several reproducibility details are missing or unclear: how QA pairs are generated from warning text, how Chinese warning text is translated/normalized, how the 4D 185-channel tensor is mapped into the base VLM input, and what role the 'Vision Encoder' plays in Figure 2. Dataset and code are promised but not yet available for inspection.

The 'physically consistent' claims are supported mainly by qualitative visualizations rather than quantitative validation, and the paper does not show that the model learns physically meaningful relationships rather than dataset artifacts. The LLM-as-a-judge protocol may introduce evaluator bias and lacks human validation.

Geographic and temporal coverage is limited: training is on China-only data from 2023-2024, with cross-regional testing on only 1,000 U.S. samples. This limits conclusions about global generalization and long-term robustness.

strengths: Introduces MP-Bench, a genuinely large-scale (421,363 pairs) multimodal dataset for severe weather that, unlike prior work (CrisisLex, ClimateIQA, CLLMate, OmniEarth), pairs raw 4D ERA5 reanalysis fields (37 pressure levels, 5 variables) with textual severe-weather warnings, and preserves original temporal and vertical structure rather than collapsing to daily averages and RGB pseudo-images. This addresses a real gap and is a reusable community resource.

The three plug-and-play modules (DTGF, TGS, TGCA) are cleanly motivated and individually ablated. The temporal-window ablation (Table 4, Table 7) and the interpretability analyses in Figs. 7-8 (e.g., 500 hPa meridional wind and 850 hPa zonal wind receiving high channel weights, DTGF assigning early time-steps higher weight for red warnings) are interesting and plausibly connect learned attention to known synoptic-scale reasoning.

Empirical results are consistent and non-trivial: all four MMLM variants beat their corresponding baselines on every task, with the Qwen2.5-VL variant gaining ~16 points MC accuracy and nearly doubling Macro-F1, and the module-combination ablation shows complementary gains (Table 3). Cross-geographical generalization to NOAA Storm Events (64.2% Acc / 35.2% Macro-F1) is a reasonable external-validity check.

Four complementary QA formats (MC, T/F, RSW, NSW) with a documented 2023/2024 train-test split, class-balance statistics (Table 5), and prompt templates (Figs. 10-13) provide a concrete, reproducible evaluation protocol, and the authors commit to releasing code and data.
weaknesses: The central framing as severe weather *prediction* / early warning is not supported by the experimental setup. The input window [t, t+11] starts at the warning issuance time and is described as 'ERA5 reanalysis data from 12 hours post-severe weather warning issuance,' so the model is classifying meteorological fields that are largely concurrent with (and partially derived from the same observations underlying) the already-issued warning. This is a diagnosis/interpretation task, not forecasting, and it substantially weakens the motivation, the title, and the claim of an 'automated early-warning pipeline.'

The evaluation methodology is weak in places. NSW is scored by GPT-4o LLM-as-a-judge on a 0-5 rubric (Fig. 14), which is noisy and not validated against human experts at scale. More importantly, the strongest comparison is only against general-purpose VLMs (LLaVA, InternVL, Qwen2.5-VL, GPT-4o) fine-tuned on 3-channel inputs; there is no comparison against meteorological-appropriate baselines (NWP post-processing, precipitation nowcasting, or gridded forecasting models like HR-Extreme / FengWu-style systems), so it is unclear whether the MLLM approach adds value over standard meteorological practice.

The absolute performance on the most informative metric is low and under-discussed. MMLM's best MC-sub Macro-F1 is only 11.83 and MC-main Macro-F1 50.88, and NSW scores top out at 2.1/5. These numbers indicate the task is far from solved and that rare-category discrimination remains poor, which somewhat undercuts the claim of 'strong performance' and 'effective severe weather understanding.'

Several claims are over-stated relative to related work. The assertion that 'this is the first time MLLM has been used to deeply interpret raw meteorological data and generate warning conclusions in sentence form' is hard to sustain given WeatherQA, ClimateIQA, CLLMate, and OmniEarth-Bench (which the paper itself cites), and the '4D' ingestion claim is partially weakened because TGCA reduces the 185 channels via attention and the fused output is mapped through an MLP to a 2D-friendly LLM input.

Presentation and reproducibility issues: the ablation study is conducted on only 5,000 samples, geographic coverage is essentially China-only (US used only as a 1,000-sample generalization probe), reference formatting is inconsistent (e.g., 'Llm' vs 'LLM', duplicated/duplicated-looking entries), and the manuscript contains typos ('cores' for 'scores'). The contribution would be stronger with a clearer statement of the forecasting-vs-diagnosis distinction and expert validation of the NSW judge.

strengths: Introduces MP-Bench, a large-scale dataset with 421,363 QA pairs built from 2023-2024 CMA severe weather warnings and ERA5 reanalysis, covering seven severe weather types and four QA task formats (MC, T/F, RSW, NSW). If released, this could be a useful benchmark for multimodal severe-weather understanding.

Proposes MMLM, which integrates three plug-and-play modules for temporal (DTGF), spatial (TGS), and vertical/channel (TGCA) feature extraction. The architecture is clearly described and directly targets high-dimensional meteorological inputs.

Reports consistent improvements over open-source MLLM baselines on MP-Bench (Table 2), e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct improves from 56.26 to 72.37 MC-main accuracy and from 68.33 to 87.13 T/F accuracy when augmented with the proposed modules.

Provides ablation studies (Table 3) showing that each proposed module contributes to performance on a 5,000-sample subset, and a temporal-window ablation (Table 4) supporting the choice of a 12-hour window over 1h and 6h windows.

Includes supplementary material with training/evaluation hyperparameters (Tables 8-9), QA prompt examples, a GPT-4o scoring rubric, and visualizations of module weight patterns that offer qualitative insight into model behavior.
Addresses an important and timely application area with potential societal impact for severe weather early warning and disaster mitigation.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear descriptions of the dataset construction pipeline, model components, and experimental settings.
weaknesses: A critical methodological flaw: the dataset and experiments use ERA5 reanalysis for the 12 hours after warning issuance to predict/explain a warning issued at time t. Future reanalysis data would not be available in real time for early warning. This makes the setup retrospective rather than forecasting and invalidates the central claim of an operational AI-driven severe weather warning system.

The main comparison is confounded: baselines are fine-tuned on 3-channel meteorological inputs, while MMLM uses 185 channels (5 variables x 37 pressure levels). The reported gains may largely reflect additional input information rather than the proposed modules. A fair comparison would give baselines the same 185-channel input or compare MMLM without modules on the full dataset.

Ablation Table 3 uses only 5,000 samples and its all-modules-off baseline (MC-main Acc 42.73) is inconsistent with the Qwen2.5-VL baseline in Table 2 (56.26). The ablation therefore does not clearly isolate the modules' contribution under the same data/training regime as the main results.

No comparison is provided against established numerical weather prediction systems or specialized AI weather forecasting models (e.g., Pangu-Weather, GraphCast, FuXi) or operational warning baselines. This makes the claimed superiority and practical value unsupported.

The dataset's text is templated QA derived from structured CMA warning records (location, type, severity, time), not naturally occurring textual warnings or forecast discussions. This limits semantic richness and weakens the 'multimodal' and 'language understanding' claims.

Evaluation has significant gaps: NSW (open-ended national warning) scores only 2.1/5, NSW constitutes only ~0.4% of the dataset, and GPT-4o is used as an LLM judge without human validation or analysis of judge bias. No confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported.

Technical inconsistencies and errors: the main text lists precipitation and pressure as 37-level variables, but Table 6 lists only z, u, v, t, q; '185 pressure levels' actually refers to 185 channels (5 variables x 37 levels); and notation/dimensions in the equations (e.g., X in DTGF vs. TGCA) are not fully consistent.

Overclaims: 'first large-scale multimodal dataset' and 'first time that MLLM has been used to deeply interpret raw meteorological data' are questionable given prior datasets such as WeatherQA, ClimateIQA, CLLMate, and OmniEarth-Bench. ERA5 is also not 'raw' meteorological data but a reanalysis product.

Reproducibility is limited: code and dataset are not yet available, and the paper does not fully specify negative-sample selection, QA generation, exact prompts for all tasks, NOAA cross-regional adaptation details, or the exact training-set sizes used for the ablation.

The proposed modules are relatively simple and incremental (temporal gating, Gaussian spatial mask, text-conditioned channel attention). Their novelty for a top computer vision venue is limited, and the paper reads more as an application/dataset contribution suited to a geoscience or climate-focused venue.

Cross-geographical generalization is only tested on 1,000 NOAA samples, and the paper does not report the corresponding baseline numbers in a table or discuss why the model still achieves 64.20% accuracy despite domain shift.

The paper does not validate real-world utility: no deployment or latency analysis, no use of forecast fields, and no discussion of how the model would handle imperfect NWP forecasts, missing data, or operational constraints.
